positions.commentary: The speaker highlights NVIDIA's massive long-term growth from $6 to $28, describing its chart as a 'big swooping hyperbola upward' rather than a parabola, illustrating that winners keep winning.
The speaker uses the 'snap test' to argue that Amazon is so deeply ingrained in the world that if it disappeared overnight, everyone would notice, making it a huge indicator for long-term ownership.
Tesla is cited as one of the great companies of our time, being a top dog and first mover in an important emerging industry, and the speaker deeply respects entrepreneurs who get a company public.
The speaker notes that while Twitter hasn't been a great stock, it has been an amazing business driven by entrepreneurship.
Starbucks is cited as a top dog and first mover in an important emerging industry, and the speaker notes that Howard Schultz was a visionary CEO who talked about Starbucks being the third place.
Amgen is cited as an example of a company with optionality, where it invented epigen, a blood substitute initially approved for one instance, but then turned out to work in another instance as well.

Google is cited as an example of a company that looked overvalued initially because people questioned how it would make money with a free search engine, but it turned out to be a beautiful thing with huge advertising potential.
The speaker describes Facebook as a rule breaker that shook the earth when born and notes that it is currently shaking the earth with two billion people using it daily.

thesis: This episode argues that investors should seek out companies that 'break the rules' and possess significant optionality, where initial market skepticism about their business model turns out to be a mispricing. The speaker emphasizes that true winners often follow a 'hyperbola upward' growth curve rather than a parabola, rewarding long-term ownership despite early overvaluation fears. Additionally, the discussion highlights the importance of identifying 'top dog' first movers in emerging industries and respecting entrepreneurs who successfully take companies public.

claims.quote: I recommended it in 2005 at 6. It went to 42 years later. It dropped to 5, one year after that. I didn't feel very good about that. My, watching my six-bagger fizzle. And then it kind of crawled back to 28th through the wreck that was 2008, 9, and into 10.
